summary:
Chubut is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework, which remains among the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Implementation at national level has also deteriorated. Trans people hired under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and INADI, the federal anti-discrimination agency, was abolished, removing the national complaints channel. Activists interviewed in Buenos Aires in April 2025 by the Washington Blade reported that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since President Milei took office, and that it is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces where Chubut is located.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a ten-year record and a 62% increase year on year, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, beatings were the main modality, institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims. Chubut sits under that national picture with no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator is therefore not applied in that case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.
tangentialFactors:
The most acute documented deterioration is concentrated in the national capital and its surroundings: trans activists interviewed in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and for Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Those same interviews place the worst police violence against trans and travesti sex workers outside the capital, in the more conservative interior provinces, which is the category Chubut belongs to.

The direction of travel is measurable rather than impressionistic: hate crime figures rose 62% year on year to a ten-year record, and institutional violence nearly quadrupled in twelve months. Against that, the underlying statute has not been repealed, and Argentina retains regional firsts including the 2010 marriage equality law, so the narrowing operates through executive decrees, budget and agency decisions rather than through legislation.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chubut change their legal gender under Law 26.743 through the civil registry process, without surgery, hormone treatment or a judge's authorisation, and the same route applies to the gender marker on the national identity document.

Public-sector and publicly funded employment is covered by the 1% Trans Labor Quota, though trans workers hired under that quota have been dismissed at national level. Anti-discrimination complaints previously went to INADI; that federal agency has been abolished, leaving residents to rely on provincial anti-discrimination mechanisms and on the courts.

The February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors restricts access for adolescents nationwide, and the second decree regulates how transgender prisoners are housed.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources available here do not record the outcome of the litigation filed against the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors; whether the decree was upheld, suspended or struck down is unresolved.

Whether INADI's abolition has been challenged in court, and whether any judicial review has followed, is not sourced. Likewise, the terms on which the 1% Trans Labor Quota dismissals were carried out and whether reinstatement has been sought are not documented.

Chubut-specific reporting is absent from this inventory: no local hate-crime figures, no provincial police-violence records and no Chubut institutional data are sourced. The national 2025 totals are the only available measure, and the absence of a provincial reporting infrastructure means separate records for Chubut cannot be generated from these sources.

Whether the national decree on the housing of transgender prisoners binds the province's own prisons, which are administered at provincial level, is not addressed in the sources.
